name: Chitral Kalasha
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress is lexical and can fall on virtually any syllable, but some lexical items exhibit variable stress. The following minimal pair illustrates the stress contrast: /ˈpaɫ̪aw/ pal'aw '(he) falls', /paˈɫ̪aw/ pal'aw 'apple'. In our data, stressed vowels are characterized by overall higher pitch (see Mørch & Heegaard 1997: 55–57), longer duration, and greater amplitude. [...] It should be noted that this generalization holds for words uttered in isolation, where pitch contours reflect a combination of stress and (declarative statement) intonation. A more systematic study of stress in Kalasha is required to determine if the generalization holds in connected speech.
new_statements.citation: Kochetov, Alexei, Paul Arsenault, Jan Heegård Petersen, Sikandar Kalas & Taj Khan Kalash. 2021. Kalasha (Bumburet variety). Illustrations of the IPA. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(3): 468-489. doi:10.1017/S0025100319000367
new_statements.locator: p. 482, section 'Prosody' (PDF page 15 of the saved file); continuation p. 483
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically specified (contrastive) and not positionally predictable: it can fall on virtually any syllable of the word, with minimal pairs such as 'paɫaw '(he) falls' vs pa'ɫaw 'apple'; some words have variable stress placement. Acoustic correlates (one speaker, elicited words): higher f0, longer duration (unstressed vowels about 30% shorter), greater amplitude, and centralization of unstressed vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: Some lexical items exhibit variable stress. Kalasha is not generally counted as a tone language, but Bashir (2003: 851) is reported (p. 483) to have noted 'salient pitch/tone contours' in northern Kalasha; the authors observe f0 differences after aspirated/breathy consonants and call for closer study of pitch variation. Vowel length is tied to stress and is generally not phonemic (Bashir 1988:35 and Heegård & Mørch 2004 leave limited length contrast open).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; the acoustic generalization is explicitly restricted to words uttered in isolation (citation forms), with connected speech left for future study. Data from two male speakers of the Bumburet-valley variety.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes the Bumburet-valley variety of Kalasha (two male speakers). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect children under kala1372, so no separate glottocode applies; the statement is taken as valid for Chitral Kalasha (kala1372) as a whole, noting that Bashir 2003:851 is reported to mention pitch/tone contours specifically in 'northern Kalasha'. Not to be confused with Kalasha-ala (Waigali, Nuristani).
